title: Product Slop Is a Leadership Problem
author: Business Leader Daily
summary: Drawing on an HBR IdeaCast conversation with Cisco's chief product officer Jeetu Patel, this post argues that once AI makes building features nearly free, the scarce leadership skill is deciding what deserves to exist. The author extends the idea of AI slop to products: features shipped because they sounded cool, settings nobody asked for, the fourth dashboard. Stacked up, these bury the few things customers care about, and users can only absorb so many new capabilities in a year. Engineering time used to force hard prioritization arguments, and that limit is disappearing, so a team that could build ten things can now build two hundred. The advice is to start from what the customer is trying to get done, build the smallest set of things that fixes it, and build them properly.
points: When building and shipping are close to free, the scarce leadership skill becomes deciding what deserves to exist.
Product slop is the feature that shipped because it sounded cool, such as an unrequested setting or a fourth dashboard.
Too many mediocre features bury the two or three things customers value most.
Engineering time used to force prioritization, and that constraint is vanishing as teams can build far more.
The remedy is to start with the customer's unmet need, build the smallest set that solves it, and do it properly.
quotes: When building code and shipping features is close to free, the scarce thing is deciding what deserves to exist.
Great leaders decide what not to build before they decide what to build.
Every one of them looked interesting in the planning meeting. Stack them up, and they bury the two or three things your customer cares most about.
A team that could build ten things can now build two hundred. And once you can build two hundred things, somebody will suggest building all of them to see what sticks.
Going from three things a day to ten doesn’t change much, he said. Doing those three things far better does.
Your users can only digest and learn so many new features over a month, a quarter, or a year.
What is our customer trying to get done, and where is it still too hard? Then build the smallest set of things that fixes that, and build those things properly.
